transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date/Time: 2025-12-03 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maria Gonzalez (Atlas - Head of ML), Ethan Park (Atlas - VP Eng), Samir Patel (Atlas - Data Eng)

Summary (auto-generated): Discussed cost/unit economics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private; key levers: batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization. Customer requested pricing spreadsheet, security docs, and sample-driven benchmark.

Topics: pricing per-token, batching/caching impact, dedicated capacity tradeoffs, private deployment constraints, security/compliance (SOC2/KMS), POC next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this deal. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick intros?
[00:07] Maria: Hi Jordan, Maria here, head of ML at Atlas. We're mainly evaluating economics—want to see where Redwood fits versus hosted options and our own infra.
[00:12] Ethan: Ethan, VP Eng. I'm here for cost and ops questions.
[00:15] Samir: Samir, data eng, I'll be running the POC if we move forward.
[00:18] Priya: Great — quick agenda: go over your workload, we sketch per-token cost, show levers (batching, caching, quant), and then map hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:25] Maria: Sounds good. Our usage: about 1M requests/month, avg prompt 120 tokens in, 280 tokens out — so roughly 400 tokens total on average. Peak QPS around 30 rps, steady-state 5–8. Budget is tight, looking to cap infra cost to ~ $20k/month initially.
[00:42] Jordan: Helpful. So rough math: at our hosted rates, naively per-token pricing x volume equals X — but big caveat is batching and KV cache can reduce unit cost a lot. Priya, want to walk through an example?
[00:50] Priya: Yeah. If we assume naive hosted price of $0.0006 per token (example), 1M requests * 400 tokens would be 400M tokens ~ $240k — clearly way above their budget. But with batching and prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts, plus using a smaller model for some paths, effective tokens billed or served can drop.
[01:12] Maria: Wait, that $0.0006 is similar to public APIs, right? We're trying to compare hosted Redwood vs self-hosted GPUs and dedicated Redwood.
[01:18] Jordan: Exactly. Two things: 1) Hosted provides simple per-token billing but we offer recommendations — you can get quoted committed rates for higher volume or go to dedicated capacity which gives a predictably lower per-token when amortized. 2) Private deployments let you control infra — cost base shifts to hardware + ops.
[01:30] Priya: For example, with batching—if your workload allows 4x effective batch size during peaks, you can reduce GPU overhead per token. And with Redwood's KV cache for common prefixes (like system prompts or repeated user context), we can short-circuit a lot of computation. In practice, we've seen 30–60% token cost reduction on chat workloads with high repetition.
[01:51] Ethan: How deterministic is that? Our prompts vary a lot but we do have a set of canned system prompts and some repeated question templates.
[01:58] Priya: Not every workload will get 60%, that's optimistic. More conservative is 20–35% unless you have heavy repetition. Also quantization: 4-bit or 8-bit can drop serving cost; for dedicated/private you can use quantized kernels which reduce GPU memory and improve throughput.
[02:15] Maria: Can you walk numbers for our profile? 1M reqs/month, 400 tokens average, target $20k/month.
[02:22] Jordan: Sure—quick back-of-envelope. At $0.00006 per token you'd be at $24k — wait hold on, let me rephrase — (laughter). To hit $20k with 400M tokens means we need effective cost ~ $0.00005 per token. That usually implies either committed/dedicated pricing, effective batching, or a hybrid where embeddings or non-critical paths use cheaper models.
[02:45] Samir: Are you mixing per-input and per-output tokens? We have longer outputs on some flows.
[02:49] Priya: We try to bill both directions but when we talk about cost optimization we look at reducing model tokens generated (e.g., truncation, post-processing) and increasing cache hits. Also route some calls to smaller models for low-value responses.
[03:03] Maria: For Dedicated, what's the typical commit and how do you price the dedicated GPU pools?
[03:09] Jordan: Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — you commit to a capacity tier monthly/annually. Pricing is a flat capacity fee + a much lower per-token usage fee sometimes, depending on contract. The more you commit, the better unit economics because the infra is amortized. We can send a tiered spreadsheet.
[03:24] Priya: Important note: Dedicated also gives you control over batching windows and kernel selection, so throughput improvements are larger compared to noisy multi-tenant hosted.
[03:33] Ethan: Private (VPC/on-prem) — what's the ops lift? We have compliance needs, but people here would rather avoid huge ops overhead.
[03:41] Priya: Private options: 1) VPC-hosted private control plane where Redwood manages runtime but network/VPC connects to you — less ops. 2) Full on-prem package — we ship artefacts/scripts and you manage infra. On-prem gives lowest recurring ops costs if you already have GPU infra, but higher upfront integration and ongoing patching. Also KMS/HSM integrations for keys.
[04:00] Maria: Security is a must — SOC2, SSO (SAML or OIDC), audit logs, customer-managed KMS.
[04:06] Jordan: We support SOC2 attestation, SAML SSO, RBAC, and can plug into KMS for private deployments. Priya will share the security pack after the call.
[04:15] Samir: For the POC, we need to simulate peak QPS and test KV cache hit rates. What's the best way to provide sample prompts?
[04:22] Priya: Send a sample of your traffic distribution (top prompts, frequency), and ideally a histogram of sequence lengths. We can run a bench that mirrors your QPS and show effective tokens and latency. That will allow us to give a focused estimate for batching gains.
[04:33] Maria: One question on batching windows — what's the latency trade? We can't add more than 50–100ms to tail latencies.
[04:39] Priya: Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs — you can set a max batch wait (e.g., 20–50ms) and a target tail latency. The system balances throughput vs latency. If you need strict low tail p99, batching gains shrink but you still get some improvement at higher batch concurrency.
[04:57] Ethan: Any examples where customers hit their $20k target?
[05:00] Jordan: Yes — we worked with a mid-market fintech that had heavy repetition, committed to dedicated, and used caching + model routing; they saw 3x improvement vs naive hosted costs. But that's workload dependent.
[05:11] Maria: We use some wrappers that add a 40-token context consistently — that seems like a good caching opportunity?
[05:16] Priya: Exactly — repeated contexts are golden for KV cache. Also recommend evaluating prompt templates to compress repeated metadata into shorter tokens or store as external context to reduce per-request tokens.
[05:27] Samir: On quantization — if we go dedicated/private, are there quality regressions with 4-bit?
[05:32] Priya: Possible but often minimal for many models. We run evals and regressions tests. For sensitive outputs we can route to higher-precision models. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles per workload.
[05:45] Ethan: What about fallbacks if dedicated capacity is exhausted?
[05:49] Jordan: We have routing policies — failover to hosted or burst capacity, and automatic model variant fallback. All configurable in the Console.
[05:56] Maria: Can you also show cost model with a hybrid: hosted for non-critical, dedicated for core workload?
[06:01] Jordan: Absolutely — that's a common approach. We'll produce a model showing blended unit economics given your traffic split.
[06:07] Priya: For the POC, ideally provide: traffic sample, top 50 prompts, SLAs, and any compliance constraints. We'll run bench and show expected token consumption after caching/batching/quantization.
[06:18] Ethan: About SLA — do you offer uptime/latency SLAs on Dedicated?
[06:22] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets, depending on the contract tier.
[06:28] Maria: Anything else on pricing nuance? e.g., embeddings vs generation costs?
[06:32] Priya: Embeddings are usually lower cost and billed differently; if you offload some tasks to embeddings + vector DB, you can reduce generation tokens. Also we have recommendations to cache embedding vectors for repeated queries.
[06:45] Samir: Who should we expect to be on the POC calls from Redwood?
[06:48] Jordan: Me and Priya for first two sessions; we may bring an infra engineer if there are low-level perf tweaks.
[06:54] Maria: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[06:56] Jordan: Recap: Jordan sends pricing spreadsheet with hosted/dedicated/private compare + blended unit economics scenarios; Priya sends security pack and POC benchmark plan; Atlas provides traffic samples and top prompts; we schedule POC kickoff for mid-December.
[07:10] Ethan: Sounds good. Any questions from anyone?
[07:13] Maria: No, thanks — please include sample assumptions in the spreadsheet (batch sizes, cache hit rates, quant levels).
[07:20] Jordan: Will do. Thanks all.
[07:22] Meeting ends.

Notes about transcription: some product names auto-transcribed (e.g., KV cache -> "K V cash" in earlier drafts), small mis-hears on model names and numbers. Action items and next steps captured above.
